summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands is a United States territory and stands under the full federal framework of the United States, which governs entry, travel documents and airport screening for anyone arriving in or leaving the islands. Those federal rules apply in the territory as they do elsewhere in the United States and are set out in the national record; what follows is the territorial layer.

The territory's human-rights law bars discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, so a trans visitor has a territorial statutory protection against discrimination while in the islands.

Marriage is available in the territory. In 2015 the territorial Superior Court struck down the denial of marriage licences to same-sex couples, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex under birth-sex status can obtain a licence in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

The historic sodomy statute, applied in the territory from 1957, has been replaced; no criminalisation of same-sex conduct remains on the territorial books.
tangentialFactors:
The human-rights law's coverage of gender identity was confirmed for territorial schools by the Attorney General's 2017 interpretation, so its application to other territorial institutions rests on the same reading of the statute.

The replacement of the sodomy statute removed the last territorial criminal provision directed at same-sex conduct. Legal exposure for a trans visitor now turns on federal entry and screening rules rather than on the territory's own criminal law.
localsOnly:
In March 2017 the territory's Attorney General ruled that the territorial anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, an official interpretation that carries the human-rights law into the islands' schools.

The 2015 marriage ruling was issued by the territorial Superior Court, so the licence route for residents runs through the territory's own courts rather than through a mainland proceeding.
outOfScopeNotes:
Reporting from July 2017 described setbacks for the territory's LGBTQ community alongside prospects for change; the specific measures at issue are not identified in the available material and remain unresolved.

No territorial provision or enforcement record on visitor-facing matters such as access to sex-segregated facilities, hate-crime prosecution, or police treatment of trans people was identified.

Whether the territorial human-rights law provides a complaint route open to non-resident visitors is not sourced.
